text: More than 100 years ago, Walter Gropius started an art school in Germany called the Bauhaus.
He wanted to bring all the arts together and to train artists to work with industry, the makers of goods.
src: Walter Gropius founded the Bauhaus in Weimar in 1919 / Germany: Weimar
to bring all the arts together and to train artists to work with industry

text: Bauhaus designs had no decoration, just simple shapes, rounded corners and long rows of windows.
The Bauhaus product that earned the most money was its wallpaper.
src: the absence of ornament / simple geometric shapes, rounded corners, curved chrome pipes and long banks of windows
The most profitable product of the Bauhaus, a school remembered for its chairs and buildings, was its wallpaper

text: Famous painters taught there, such as Paul Klee and Wassily Kandinsky.
First-year students learned about design and colour and tried out different materials.
src: the painters Paul Klee, Wassily Kandinsky and Lyonel Feininger
first-year students learnt the elements of design and colour theory and experimented with materials

text: The school had to move from Weimar to Dessau, and then to Berlin.
The Nazis called it “un-German”, and under their pressure the school closed itself.
src: Driven out of Weimar in 1925 and Dessau in 1932 / Weimar (1919–1925), Dessau (1925–1932) and Berlin (1932–1933)
the school was closed by its own leadership in Berlin in 1933 under pressure from the Nazis, whose writers had labelled it “un-German”

text: Its teachers carried its ideas to Britain, the United States and Tel Aviv.
In Dessau, apartment buildings it built are still in use, and several Bauhaus sites are World Heritage sites.
src: Its émigré teachers carried its ideas to Britain, the United States and Tel Aviv
the balcony-access apartment buildings in Dessau, still in use / Four Bauhaus sites in Germany were inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List
